subject: history
title: The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763)
dek: In December 755 An Lushan, a frontier general who commanded three of the Tang empire's northern armies, marched south from Fanyang near today's Beijing. Within seven months he held both Tang capitals, the emperor had fled to Sichuan, and the emperor's favourite consort, Yang Guifei, had been put to death by his own guards. The war dragged on for eight years. The Tang dynasty survived, but it never again controlled its own provinces the way it had before, and the shock of the war shaped Chinese poetry, calligraphy and politics for centuries.
honesty: Most of what we know comes from histories written later by the Tang's own side and its successors, especially the Old and New Books of Tang and Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian, which treat An Lushan as a villain and Yang Guifei's family as the root of the trouble. Treat the vivid personal details about An Lushan with some caution. The often-repeated claim that the rebellion killed about 36 million people comes from comparing a census of 755 (about 52.9 million registered people) with one of 764 (about 16.9 million). Most historians think much of that gap reflects a collapse of tax registration and lost provinces rather than deaths, so this lesson does not give a death toll. Western calendar dates follow the standard conversions in modern scholarship and can differ by a few days between sources. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Xuanzong takes the throne
timeline.detail: Emperor Xuanzong begins a reign of more than forty years. The first half, the Kaiyuan era, is remembered as the high point of Tang power and prosperity.

timeline.label: An Lushan becomes a military governor
timeline.detail: An Lushan is made jiedushi (military governor) of Pinglu in the northeast. He later adds Fanyang (744) and Hedong (751).

timeline.label: Yang Guifei becomes Precious Consort
timeline.detail: Yang Yuhuan is given the title Guifei. Her relatives rise at court, above all her cousin Yang Guozhong.

timeline.label: Battle of Talas
timeline.detail: A Tang army under Gao Xianzhi is defeated by Abbasid forces in Central Asia. In the same year Tang campaigns against Nanzhao in the southwest also go badly.

timeline.label: Yang Guozhong becomes chief minister
timeline.detail: After Li Linfu dies, Yang Guozhong takes over the government and becomes An Lushan's open rival.

timeline.label: The revolt begins
timeline.detail: An Lushan marches south from Fanyang, claiming he has been ordered to remove Yang Guozhong.

timeline.label: Luoyang falls; Yan dynasty declared
timeline.detail: The eastern capital falls in about a month. An Lushan proclaims himself emperor of a new Great Yan dynasty.

timeline.label: Tong Pass, flight, and Mawei
timeline.detail: Geshu Han is ordered out of the Tong Pass defences, and his army is destroyed. Xuanzong flees west; at Mawei station his guards kill Yang Guozhong and force the emperor to have Yang Guifei killed. Rebels take Chang'an.

timeline.label: Suzong enthroned at Lingwu
timeline.detail: The crown prince Li Heng is proclaimed emperor in the northwest. Xuanzong, in Sichuan, accepts his son's accession.

timeline.label: An Lushan murdered
timeline.detail: An Lushan, ill, nearly blind and violent toward his own staff, is killed by a plot involving his son An Qingxu.

timeline.label: Suiyang and the recapture of the capitals
timeline.detail: Zhang Xun's garrison holds Suiyang for most of the year, blocking the road south. With Uyghur cavalry, Tang forces retake Chang'an and Luoyang late in the year.

timeline.label: Salt monopoly and a famous draft
timeline.detail: The court creates a state salt monopoly to raise money. Yan Zhenqing writes his draft requiem for his nephew killed in the war.

timeline.label: Shi Siming takes over
timeline.detail: After the Tang siege of Yecheng collapses, Shi Siming kills An Qingxu and becomes the Yan emperor.

timeline.label: Shi Siming murdered
timeline.detail: Shi Siming is killed on the orders of his son Shi Chaoyi.

timeline.label: The rebellion ends
timeline.detail: Cornered and abandoned by his generals, Shi Chaoyi kills himself. Surrendered Yan generals are allowed to keep their armies in Hebei.

timeline.label: Tibetans occupy Chang'an
timeline.detail: Taking advantage of Tang weakness, Tibetan forces briefly occupy the capital.

timeline.label: The two-tax law
timeline.detail: Chief minister Yang Yan replaces the old per-person tax system with taxes on property and land, collected twice a year.

timeline.label: The end of the Tang
timeline.detail: After the Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) and decades of warlord power, the last Tang emperor is deposed.

sections.title: A golden age with a weak point on the frontier

blocks.text: When Emperor Xuanzong came to the throne in 712, the Tang dynasty was almost a century old. Its capital, Chang'an, was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people inside and around its walls. Merchants from Central Asia, Persia and Korea lived there, Buddhist monks travelled to and from India and Japan, and the court collected taxes from a registered population of more than fifty million. The first part of Xuanzong's reign, the Kaiyuan era, is still remembered in Chinese as a model of good government.

The weak point was the army. Early Tang China had relied on farmer-soldiers who served in rotation and went home. As the empire pushed into Central Asia, Manchuria and the southwest, that system could not keep enough men on distant borders. The court replaced it with large professional armies stationed permanently on the frontier, each commanded by a jiedushi, or military governor. By the 740s there were ten of these commands, and together they held most of the empire's trained troops. The capital region itself had relatively few.

Over time the jiedushi gained control not only of soldiers but of supplies, local finances and appointments. Xuanzong's long-serving chief minister Li Linfu preferred to give these commands to non-Han career soldiers rather than to scholar-officials, partly because such men had no family network at court and could not become political rivals. The policy made sense for Li Linfu's own position. It also placed huge armies in the hands of men whose loyalty rested on the emperor's personal favour.

In the second half of his reign Xuanzong grew less interested in daily government. He devoted himself to music, Daoism and, from the 740s, to Yang Yuhuan, who became his Precious Consort, Yang Guifei. Her relatives were promoted and enriched. When Li Linfu died in 752, her cousin Yang Guozhong took over as chief minister. Meanwhile the empire suffered defeats on the frontier: at Talas in Central Asia in 751, and in costly campaigns against the kingdom of Nanzhao in the southwest.

sections.title: Why historians call this a turning point

blocks.text: Chinese historians usually call the war the An–Shi Rebellion, after its two main leaders, An Lushan and Shi Siming. It is often treated as the dividing line between the early Tang and the late Tang, and sometimes as the dividing line between early imperial China and later imperial China.

The reason is not that the Tang fell. It did not. The reason is that the war changed how the empire worked. Before 755, the court in Chang'an appointed officials, registered households and taxed them directly across most of the country. After 763, large regions were run by military governors who passed their posts to sons or chosen officers, kept their own taxes, and obeyed the court only when it suited them. The court survived by relying on the rich south, on state monopolies such as salt, and on its own palace armies, which were increasingly controlled by eunuchs.

items: Military power moved from the centre to the provinces. The jiedushi system that caused the war became the normal form of government in much of the north.
The economic centre of China began moving south. The Yangzi region was barely touched by the fighting and became the court's main source of revenue.
The empire lost Central Asia. Troops were withdrawn to fight the rebels, and Tibet and the Uyghurs took over much of the western frontier.

Attitudes toward foreigners hardened. Because An Lushan and many of his officers were of Sogdian, Turkic or other non-Han origin, the war fed suspicion of outsiders in a society that had been unusually open.
Literature changed. Poets such as Du Fu wrote about war, refugees and conscription in a direct, personal way that later readers saw as poetry bearing witness to history.

sections.title: An emperor, a consort, two rebel dynasties and their opponents

people.name: Xuanzong
people.text: Tang emperor from 712 to 756. He presided over the dynasty's height and the beginning of its crisis. He trusted An Lushan, lost both capitals, and abdicated in favour of his son after fleeing to Sichuan. He returned to Chang'an in 757 and lived out his final years with little power.

people.name: Yang Guifei
people.text: Xuanzong's Precious Consort and one of the most famous women in Chinese history. Traditional histories blame her family for the disaster, and later stories even claimed she adopted An Lushan as a son. She was killed at Mawei in July 756 when the emperor's guards demanded her death. Later poets turned her into a tragic heroine.

people.name: An Lushan
people.text: A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic background from the northeastern borderlands. He rose through skill as a soldier and interpreter, and through his talent for winning Xuanzong's favour. By 751 he commanded the Pinglu, Fanyang and Hedong armies. He rebelled in 755, declared himself emperor of Yan in 756, and was murdered in his own palace in 757.

people.name: Yang Guozhong
people.text: Yang Guifei's cousin and chief minister after 752. His rivalry with An Lushan helped push An into revolt, and his order to Geshu Han to leave the Tong Pass led to the loss of Chang'an. He was killed by soldiers at Mawei.

people.name: Shi Siming
people.text: An Lushan's comrade from the same frontier region. He briefly submitted to the Tang, rebelled again, killed An Lushan's son in 759 and ruled as emperor of Yan until his own son had him killed.

people.name: Suzong
people.text: Xuanzong's son Li Heng, who was proclaimed emperor at Lingwu in 756 and organised the Tang recovery with the generals Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi and Uyghur allies.

people.name: Guo Ziyi
people.text: The most celebrated Tang general of the war. He helped retake both capitals and later held off Tibetan and Uyghur threats. In later Chinese culture he became a symbol of the loyal, long-lived and fortunate official.

people.name: Yan Zhenqing
people.text: A scholar-official and one of the greatest calligraphers in Chinese history. As prefect of Pingyuan he raised troops against the rebels in 755–756. His cousin Yan Gaoqing and his nephew Yan Jiming were killed after Changshan fell.

people.name: Zhang Xun
people.text: The commander who defended Yongqiu and then Suiyang against rebel armies, holding the route to the south for most of 757 before the city fell and he was executed.

people.name: Du Fu
people.text: The poet who lived through the war as a minor official, a captive in occupied Chang'an and a refugee. His war poems made him known to later readers as the 'poet-historian'.

sections.title: From the march south to the end of Yan

blocks.text: An Lushan left Fanyang on 16 December 755 with an army that later accounts put at well over 100,000 men, including Turkic, Khitan and Xi cavalry. His stated aim was to rescue the emperor from Yang Guozhong. The government had few trained troops in the interior, and many local officials surrendered. The rebels crossed the Yellow River and took Luoyang, the eastern capital, in January 756. There An declared himself emperor of the Great Yan dynasty.

The court then made a series of mistakes. Xuanzong executed his generals Gao Xianzhi and Feng Changqing after they retreated, on the word of a eunuch observer. Their replacement, the veteran Geshu Han, held the narrow Tong Pass between Luoyang and Chang'an, which was the right strategy. Yang Guozhong, fearing that Geshu Han's army might be turned against him, pressed the emperor to order an attack. In early July 756 Geshu Han marched out, his army was destroyed, and the road to Chang'an lay open.

Xuanzong left the capital secretly before dawn with his family, Yang Guozhong and a guard. At Mawei station, west of the city, the hungry and angry soldiers killed Yang Guozhong and several of his relatives, then refused to go on until Yang Guifei also died. The emperor agreed, and she was strangled. Xuanzong continued to Sichuan. His son Li Heng went northwest instead, and in August officials at Lingwu proclaimed him emperor. He is known as Suzong.

The rebels occupied Chang'an but did not destroy the Tang. Loyal officials in Hebei, behind rebel lines, rose against An Lushan. Yan Zhenqing at Pingyuan and his cousin Yan Gaoqing at Changshan were among the first. Changshan was retaken by the rebels, and Yan Gaoqing was taken to Luoyang and executed. In the south, Zhang Xun's small force held first Yongqiu and then Suiyang. The siege of Suiyang lasted most of 757. The defenders ran out of food and, according to the histories, ate their horses, then birds and rats, then people. The city fell in the autumn, but by then the rebels had lost their chance to break into the Huai and Yangzi regions, which supplied the Tang with grain and money.

Inside the rebel camp, things went badly. An Lushan had become ill, nearly blind and violent toward his own servants and officials. In January 757 a group including his son An Qingxu and his attendant Li Zhu'er killed him. With cavalry from the Uyghur Khaganate, Tang forces under Suzong's son retook Chang'an and then Luoyang late in 757. The Uyghurs had been promised plunder, and they took it, especially in Luoyang.

The war could have ended there. Instead it dragged on. Shi Siming submitted to the Tang, then rebelled again. A huge Tang siege of An Qingxu at Yecheng in 758–759 collapsed because nine generals had no single commander. Shi Siming killed An Qingxu, retook Luoyang and ruled as emperor until 761, when his son Shi Chaoyi had him killed. By 762 Yan generals were changing sides. Luoyang was recaptured a second time, again with Uyghur help, and in February 763 Shi Chaoyi killed himself.

The price of the ending was a compromise. To persuade the remaining Yan generals to surrender, the court let them keep their armies and their territory as Tang military governors. In Hebei, three of these commands, usually called the three Hebei garrisons, became almost independent and stayed that way for the rest of the dynasty. The rebellion was over, but the conditions that made it possible had been written into the structure of the empire.

sections.title: A calligrapher's rough draft for a dead nephew

blocks.text: When An Lushan rebelled, Yan Zhenqing was prefect of Pingyuan in Hebei and his cousin Yan Gaoqing was prefect of nearby Changshan. Both declared for the Tang. Yan Gaoqing's son Yan Jiming carried messages between them. In early 756 rebel troops besieged Changshan. Help did not arrive, the city fell, and Yan Gaoqing and his son were killed. Yan Gaoqing was taken to Luoyang and executed after he refused to submit to An Lushan.

In 758, after Tang forces had retaken the area, Yan Zhenqing sent a relative to search for the bodies. Only Yan Jiming's head was recovered. Yan Zhenqing then wrote a short memorial text addressed to his dead nephew. It survives not as a clean copy but as a rough draft, with crossed-out words, inserted phrases and lines that grow faster and heavier as the text goes on. In one line he writes that traitorous officials did not come to the rescue, the lone city was surrounded, the father was captured and the son died.

Chinese connoisseurs came to value the draft precisely because it is unfinished. It records a man writing in grief, correcting himself as he goes. Later critics ranked it second only to Wang Xizhi's Preface to the Orchid Pavilion among works of running script. It is one of the clearest examples of how a political catastrophe entered Chinese art not through official history but through a private document.

sections.title: Eurasia in the 750s: an age of revolts and new dynasties

blocks.text: The An Lushan Rebellion happened during a period of upheaval across Eurasia. Historian Christopher Beckwith has pointed out that between about 742 and 755 most of the great states of the continent experienced a major rebellion, revolution or change of dynasty.

items: The steppe: in 742–744 the Second Turkic Khaganate was overthrown and replaced by the Uyghur Khaganate. The Uyghurs then became the Tang's indispensable and expensive allies against An Lushan.

The Islamic world: the Abbasid revolution, launched from Khurasan in 747, overthrew the Umayyad caliphate in 750. In 751 Abbasid forces defeated the Tang at Talas, and in 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad as a new capital.
Western Europe: in 751 Pepin the Short deposed the last Merovingian king and became the first Carolingian king of the Franks.
Tibet: the Tibetan emperor was assassinated in 755. His successor Trisong Detsen exploited Tang weakness after the rebellion, and Tibetan forces occupied Chang'an for about two weeks in 763.

Japan: Nara Japan was modelling its state on the Tang. The Great Buddha of Tōdaiji was consecrated in 752, and the monk Jianzhen (Ganjin) reached Japan in 753–754. The Japanese scholar Abe no Nakamaro served at the Tang court and became a friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei. When news of the rebellion reached Japan, the powerful minister Fujiwara no Nakamaro strengthened coastal defences and planned an attack on Silla; he himself died in a failed rebellion in 764.
Korea: Unified Silla was at a cultural high point. Work on Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto near Gyeongju is traditionally dated to 751.

blocks.text: The comparison with the Abbasids is especially useful. Both revolts drew on frontier armies and on networks of Sogdian and Iranian merchants and soldiers. The Abbasids won and founded a new dynasty. An Lushan's Yan dynasty failed, but the Tang that survived was a weaker, more decentralised state.

sections.title: A dynasty that lived on in a new shape

blocks.text: The Tang lasted another 144 years after the rebellion ended, so it would be wrong to say the war destroyed it. But the court never fully recovered control of the north. The surrendered Yan generals in Hebei ran their provinces as hereditary domains. Other military governors followed their example, and in 781–786 several of them rose against the court at once. In 783 a mutiny even forced Emperor Dezong to flee Chang'an.

The court adapted. The old tax system, based on registering every household and giving it equal land, had collapsed with the census. In 758 the government created a state salt monopoly, which under the official Liu Yan became one of its largest sources of income. In 780 Yang Yan's two-tax law taxed households according to their property and land, collected in summer and autumn. Historians regard this as one of the most important fiscal reforms in Chinese history, and it set the pattern for later dynasties.

There was a real recovery under Emperor Xianzong (reigned 805–820), who brought several rebellious provinces back under control. The final collapse came later, after the Huang Chao rebellion of 874–884 devastated both north and south. In 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, and China split into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. The Song dynasty, which reunified much of China in 960, deliberately kept generals under civilian control, partly because of the memory of what military governors had done to the Tang.

The war also lived on in literature. Du Fu's poems from occupied Chang'an and the refugee roads, including Spring View, Moonlit Night and the Three Officials and Three Partings, became the model for poetry about war and suffering. In 806 Bai Juyi wrote the Song of Everlasting Sorrow about Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, turning the political disaster into a love story. That poem was hugely popular in Japan; the first chapter of Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji openly compares its emperor and his doomed favourite to Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, which links this lesson to Thursday's lesson on Heian women's writing.

The traditional histories blame a few people: An Lushan for his ambition, Yang Guozhong for provoking him, Yang Guifei for distracting the emperor, and Xuanzong for neglecting government. Modern historians put more weight on the system: the court had placed most of its professional soldiers on the frontier under commanders who controlled their own money and men. If Xuanzong had been more careful and the Yang family less greedy, would the empire have avoided a war like this one, or was some kind of military revolt likely once the jiedushi system existed? And why did the women at the centre of the story, Yang Guifei above all, end up carrying so much of the blame?

fun_fact.title: The war's most famous document is in Taipei
fun_fact.text: Yan Zhenqing's Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew (祭姪文稿), written in 758 for the nephew killed after Changshan fell, is held by the National Palace Museum in Taipei. Because it is so fragile, the museum rarely displays it. When it was lent to the Tokyo National Museum for a Yan Zhenqing exhibition in early 2019, the loan caused a public argument in Taiwan and China about whether such a treasure should travel at all.
